startup.name: Termius
startup.one_liner: An SSH client with team collaboration features
startup.description: Termius is an SSH client for desktop and mobile that syncs and shares server lists, snippets and terminal sessions through an encrypted cloud vault, like a password manager for servers. Engineering and DevOps teams pay a per seat subscription. The product existed before the batch under an earlier name, so it is an existing product with some paying users rather than an idea.

yc_acceptance.basis: Start from the roughly 1.5 percent Winter 2019 rate (about 189 companies from about 12,000 applicants, per press coverage of the YC blog) and the 1 percent prior in yc_acceptance.md. Adjust up for a technical team with a shipped cross platform product and paying subscribers, and for a painful problem the founders know first hand as engineers. Adjust slightly up again because the batch grew by over 50 percent versus the previous one. Adjust down for a small niche market and a product that is an incremental upgrade to free tools. Net about 4 percent, inside the 0.3 to 15 percent guardrail.
yc_acceptance.why_it_fails: YC would most plausibly say no because an SSH client looks like a small, crowded market with free defaults (PuTTY, OpenSSH, iTerm) and a handful of paid clients, so the ceiling looks like a profitable utility rather than a venture scale company. If interviewers see only a modest installed base and no clear path from individual to team and enterprise revenue, the team collaboration pitch may not feel like a big enough wedge.

anchors.source: base_rates.py --years 2013-2018 --industry B2B --calibration-only (n=65 researched, known-only): seed 52% / 85% / 91%, cond 85% (n=40).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Within 2x of the anchor. Slightly lower than the cohort because developer tools sold to small teams are a niche and the team is outside the main US investor networks.

bands.rationale: Small angel or YC only extension round, typical for a bootstrapped tool with revenue.
Typical 2018 to 2021 B2B seed at about 2.1 to 2.5M median raise per the cohort.
Upside if Demo Day interest reflects fast growth in team seats.

ladder.why_it_fails: The most likely failure here is that Demo Day investors see a utility with a few thousand paying users and no obvious route to a large business, so the team keeps funding itself from subscription revenue and never takes an institutional seed. StackMachine and Documents.Me both entered YC with developer or security tooling and never recorded a priced round.

anchors.source: base_rates.py --years 2013-2018 --industry B2B --calibration-only (n=65 researched, known-only): series_a 26% / 42% / 65%, cond 50% (n=34).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Under the anchor by 1.8x, inside the 2x limit. The category is crowded with free tools and the paid segment is small, so conversion to a 10M plus round with the required growth is harder than the typical B2B company.

bands.rationale: Thin A led by a seed fund once revenue passes about 1M ARR.
Cohort 2018 to 2021 series A median raise 12.5M.
Upside if team plans show strong expansion and enterprise demand.

ladder.why_it_fails: Series A investors will ask for a path to tens of millions of ARR. A per seat SSH client sells to individuals and small DevOps teams, so growth may plateau near a few million dollars of revenue, below the bar. Mattermost needed a pivot to an open source collaboration platform before it raised, which shows how much distribution beyond a niche tool matters.

anchors.source: base_rates.py --years 2013-2018 --industry B2B --calibration-only (n=65 researched, known-only): series_b 20% / 32% / 58%, cond 76% (n=17).
anchors.adjustment_reason: The anchor is more than 2x higher. The cohort conditional rests on only 17 companies that had already shown strong growth, and survivors skew to larger markets. Here the niche market, and a likely plateau after an A, argue for a probability closer to a third, and the 17 company base is thin evidence.

bands.rationale: Smaller B on steady but not explosive growth.
Cohort 2018 to 2021 series B median raise about 38M.
Upside if the product expands into broader infrastructure access and security.

ladder.why_it_fails: To raise a B the company must prove it can expand from developer seats into enterprise security and access management, where well funded vendors already sell. Without that expansion, growth slows and investors decline to fund a niche utility at a B valuation. Protonet shows how a small product company can stall before a larger round.

anchors.source: base_rates.py --years 2013-2018 --industry B2B --calibration-only (n=65 researched, known-only): series_c 14% / 22% / 52%, cond 69% (n=13).
anchors.adjustment_reason: Within 2x of the anchor. Lower because few companies in a niche developer tool category reach late stage funding, and the base of 13 is small.

bands.rationale: Cohort 2018 to 2021 series C median about 59M.
Growth round if it becomes a platform for infrastructure access.
Rare late stage mega round that only a clear category leader in infrastructure access would raise.

ladder.why_it_fails: A late round needs a large, defensible platform. If the company remains a client application, bigger infrastructure access vendors or cloud providers can bundle similar features, and growth equity investors will not fund a niche tool at scale. Few companies in the B2B cohort reached series D, and those that did had far bigger markets.

outcomes.why_it_fails: Most likely the company ends as a small, profitable but stalled product, or is absorbed by a larger tooling or security vendor for a low price. The B2B cohort ended 29 percent shutdown and 42 percent acquired, but most acquisitions of niche developer tools are small. Reaching a value over a billion needs a much larger market than SSH clients alone represent.

analogs.relevance: Technical team collaboration tool sold to engineers, with open core distribution.
analogs.outcome_summary: Active, reached series B after pivoting from games.

analogs.relevance: Developer server tooling in a crowded space with free alternatives.
Security oriented tool for a niche user base with a generic name.
Small hardware and software product for teams that could not scale demand.

killers.risk: Small market and a ceiling on revenue per seat
killers.evidence: Free defaults (OpenSSH, PuTTY, iTerm) cover most needs and paid SSH clients sell mainly to a thin slice of power users and teams.
killers.mitigation: Expand into access management, auditing and compliance features that enterprises pay for.

killers.risk: Cloud and platform vendors or infrastructure access tools bundle the features
killers.evidence: Cloud consoles, browser based shells and access vendors such as Teleport already offer shared sessions and audited access.
killers.mitigation: Stay cross platform and neutral across clouds, and build deep mobile and team workflows.

killers.risk: Security trust barrier for storing server credentials in a third party vault
killers.evidence: A breach or even a perceived weakness would hurt a product whose core promise is safely holding keys and hosts.
killers.mitigation: End to end encryption, third party audits and transparent security documentation.

killers.risk: Weak individual to team conversion keeps the business a lifestyle company
killers.evidence: Individual developers use free tools and expense small sums, so growth into team and enterprise contracts is the unproven step.
killers.mitigation: Product led growth with team invites, shared vaults and snippet sharing, then outbound to DevOps leads.

competition_now.name: PuTTY and OpenSSH
competition_now.what: Free default SSH clients on Windows and Unix.
competition_now.traction: Near universal use, no team features.

competition_now.name: SecureCRT
competition_now.what: Commercial scripting oriented SSH client for professionals.
competition_now.traction: Established paid product with an enterprise base.

competition_now.name: Royal TS and iTerm2
competition_now.what: Connection managers and a popular macOS terminal.
competition_now.traction: Large user bases among administrators and Mac developers.

technical_complexity.rationale: A cross platform client with encrypted sync and shared sessions is a real engineering job, covering desktop, iOS and Android plus a zero knowledge vault and a terminal emulator. A small team can build it, but security correctness and many platforms are hard to maintain.

takeover_risk.rationale: Adding shared vaults and session links is straightforward for a funded rival, but few have the incentive for a niche client. Platform dependence on Apple and Google mobile stores is a moderate risk.

evidence.claim: Engineers manage fleets of servers and rely on SSH daily, and teams share host lists and snippets informally; paid clients exist, which shows some willingness to pay.
YC Winter 2019 drew about 12,000 applicants for about 189 places, so competition for the slot is intense.

roadmap.goal: Show a paying, growing user base and a team plan story.
actions: Publish revenue and seat growth numbers
Write a clear pitch for team and enterprise expansion
roadmap.proof: Monthly recurring revenue with a rising share from team plans

roadmap.goal: Convert YC interest into a seed with growth in team seats.
actions: Launch paid team plans with invites and shared vaults
Gather customer references from DevOps teams
roadmap.proof: Team seats growing at least 15 percent monthly at Demo Day

roadmap.goal: Reach venture scale revenue with enterprise features.
actions: Ship audit logs, SSO and access controls
roadmap.proof: About 1M to 2M annual recurring revenue with strong retention

roadmap.goal: Prove expansion beyond the client into infrastructure access.
actions: Build server side components and integrations
Sign enterprise contracts in security teams
roadmap.proof: Net revenue retention above 120 percent and several six figure contracts

roadmap.goal: Become a platform for secure infrastructure access.
actions: Expand internationally and to compliance buyers
roadmap.proof: Revenue above 20M with a clear leading position

pros.point: Technical founders with a shipped cross platform product
pros.evidence: Desktop and mobile clients with encrypted sync already exist, so the team has proven it can build.

pros.point: Bottom up developer adoption can lower sales cost
pros.evidence: SSH is used daily by engineers, so product led growth is plausible, as with Mattermost.

strengths: Short, easy to say and spell
No generic descriptor, so it is searchable
weaknesses: Does not signal SSH or terminals
Moderate recall for a dev tool
brand.rationale: An invented short name with no flags and an average cohort survival rate, so it neither helps nor hurts. Like Mattermost, a distinctive name can build recognition through a strong product, not through meaning.

narrative.headline: A plausible but niche developer tool with a modest YC chance and a ceiling set by a small market.
narrative.general_summary: Termius is an existing, revenue earning SSH client with team collaboration, sold to engineers and DevOps teams. It has a credible technical team and a real daily pain point, which helps the YC odds, but the category has free defaults and a small paid segment, so investors may see a utility rather than a venture business. Odds of reaching each round sit below the B2B cohort anchors at the later stages because the base rates come from a larger market mix. The most likely path is a seed or modest raise, a plateau around a small revenue base and an eventual small acquisition or continued independence.

assumptions: Written as of early 2019 using only the description and the public world then.
The product predated the batch, so the team is not idea stage.
Cohort used is B2B 2013 to 2018 (n=65) because the Developer Tools tag had only 5 researched companies; widened and noted.
Early 2019 SSH competitor facts are from a Wikipedia comparison and may mix later features.
Funding coverage in the data is partial, so known-only base rates are biased low and upper bounds high.
